haiku-low.q1: It does not differ. Both return the same 401 login page, "Invalid email or password", with no extra header, redirect or cookie.
haiku-low.q2: It gets a 429 login page (try again later). The password is not checked, and nothing is recorded, so the lockout is not extended.
haiku-low.q3: If the request carries the old cookie, its session row is deleted in the same transaction that creates the new session. Login never reuses an incoming ID.
haiku-low.q4: Only a random session ID: 32 random bytes, base64url-encoded. The cookie is HttpOnly, so page scripts cannot read it.
haiku-low.q5: At 12 hours after login, its absolute limit, even with constant activity. The 30-minute idle limit restarts on each request but does not extend that.
haiku-low.q6: It finds no valid row, deletes any matching session row, and returns a 302 redirect to /login with the cookie cleared. A storage error gives 503 instead.
haiku-low.q7: If a cookie was sent, the server deletes the session row matching its hash, then returns a 302 to /login with the cookie cleared. Deleting zero rows is fine, so a missing session behaves the same.
haiku-low.q8: In Postgres, shared by both instances. Any instance looks up sha256 of the cookie's session ID in the sessions table.
haiku-low.q9: In the login_failures table, one row per attempt per lowercase email with failed_at. Rows with failed_at within the last 10 minutes of Postgres now() count.
haiku-low.q10: It compares the stored hash of the session ID with idle (last_seen_at within 30 minutes) and absolute (created_at within 12 hours) limits. On success it writes last_seen_at = now() and returns user_id.
haiku-low.q11: A 503 page: "Sign-in is temporarily unavailable. Please try again in a few minutes." No cookie is set, and no session is created.
haiku-low.q12: A cleanup job every 10 minutes on each instance, guarded by pg_try_advisory_lock so only one runs it. It deletes sessions past either limit.

sonnet.q1: It doesn't differ. Same 401 status, template and text ("Invalid email or password"), no extra header, redirect or cookie. Unknown email runs bcrypt against a dummy hash so timing matches too.
sonnet.q2: The email is locked (login_lockouts row, 15 min). The attempt gets a 429 login page (try again later) without any password check; nothing is inserted, so it doesn't extend the lockout.
sonnet.q3: The old session is deleted (DELETE WHERE id_hash = sha256(old sid)) and a new session with a new random ID is created in the same transaction. The old ID is never reused.
sonnet.q4: Only the random session ID (32 random bytes, base64url) travels in the cookie. Page scripts cannot read it because the cookie is HttpOnly (also Secure, SameSite=Lax).
sonnet.q5: 12 hours after login (the absolute limit, based on created_at, which is never updated), even though the idle clock keeps restarting.
sonnet.q6: The UPDATE returns zero rows, so the server deletes any sessions row for sha256(sid), clears the sid cookie, and responds 302 redirect to /login.
sonnet.q7: If a cookie was sent, the server deletes the sessions row for sha256(sid) before responding. If the session is already gone, deleting 0 rows is fine and it behaves the same: 302 to /login with the cookie cleared.
sonnet.q8: In the Postgres sessions table (shared by both instances, no sticky sessions). Any instance hashes the cookie's ID with SHA-256 and looks up the row by id_hash in Postgres.
sonnet.q9: In the Postgres login_failures table (email, failed_at), with lockouts in login_lockouts. The window is decided by counting rows for that email whose failed_at is within the last 10 minutes (sliding window), using the database clock now().
sonnet.q10: It checks in Postgres that last_seen_at is within the last 30 minutes and created_at within the last 12 hours (using now()). When valid, it writes last_seen_at = now() in the same UPDATE, returning user_id.
sonnet.q11: A 503 page ("Sign-in is temporarily unavailable. Please try again in a few minutes.") with no cookie set.
sonnet.q12: The cleanup job, run every 10 minutes on each instance (only one does the work at a time via pg_try_advisory_lock), deletes sessions past the idle or absolute limit.
